![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223941/assets/b18b1e3a686f70a4c583324ddc253e8d334f63f017639bd47f6f483d42582801.png)

An inverted conical dispenser has a diameter of $100\,\text{in}$ and a depth of $110\,\text{in}.$ If a liquid is flowing out of the vertex of container at a rate of $9\,000\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}\text{/h}$, how fast is the height of the liquid dropping when the liquid is $60\,\text{in}$ deep?
question.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the dimensions of the container. Let's call $H=110\,\text{in}$ the height of the container, and $R=\frac{100}{2}=50\,\text{in}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the water level. We call $h$ the water level's height and $r$ the radius of the cone formed by the water. Both of these quantities, and the water volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-9\,000\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{h},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=60\,\text{in}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the container and the water must be similar. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{50}{110} \\ r & =\frac{5h}{11}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{5h}{11})}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{25}{363}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{25}{363}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{25}{121}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug in the known values, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-9\,000\pi  & =\frac{25}{121}\pi (60)^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ -9\,000\pi  & =\frac{90\,000}{121}\pi \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-12.1\,\text{in}/\text{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water height is decreasing at a rate of $12.1\,\text{in}/\text{h}.$
